en: Having prostrated before the elephant-faced Lord Gaṇeśa, the bestower of boons who is honored by all,
I shall proclaim the characteristics of duality and the rest as they are agreed upon by everyone. 1.
A consonant following a vowel undergoes doubling when another consonant follows it; likewise, a *sparśa* (stop) preceded by the letter *la*, as well as a preceding [consonant], is reduplicated.
When a consonant stands after the letter *ra* which is preceded by a vowel, [it is also doubled].
When followed by a mere consonant (*varṇamātra*), that [anusvāra] becomes two syllables (dvivarṇa).
An *anusvāra* standing after a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) should be pronounced twice when a following consonant is present. (3–4)
An *anusvāra* following a short vowel (*mātrā*) has two measures (*dvimātra*), while that following a long vowel (*dvimātrā*) has only one measure (*mātrā*).
Even when followed by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), it remains one measure, provided it possesses a double form.
An *anusvāra* has two measures when followed by the letter *r* or by sibilants (*ūṣman*).
When a subsequent sound occurs in conjunction, the *mātrika* [vowel] may become double, as in the case of *dvirūpa*.
The two sounds *na* and *ṅa*, when preceded by a short vowel and standing at the end of a word, undergo doubling;
however, this occurs only when they are followed by a vowel and joined together, and not otherwise.
Thus ends the section on doubling (dvitva).
By whatever cause doubling occurs for a consonant—namely, for a second or a fourth [consonant]—there shall be a prefixion of that [same consonant] before it. 1.
In *paramātyāti*, *bhūte*, *upasargāḥ*, *dhāma*, *pāthaḥ*, and *eṣaḥ*, this [doubling] occurs before the preceding [vowels]; and in *chakṣi* and *bhujā*, it occurs as *iyuḥ*.
In some cases, doubling occurs between two vowels according to the requirements of the observed usage.
In that regard, the preceding tradition (pūrvāgama) should be understood by those discerning in phonetics.
Thus ends the section on the preceding tradition.
Indeed, after a voiceless sibilant (ūṣman), when one remains solely upon a stop-consonant (sparśa)...
Once, that [nasalization] occurs in the same position as the contact [consonant], its first appearance being in the middle.
(1) When *s* or *ṣ* follows, whether at the end of a word or not, the first [nasal] becomes the second; however, for a [nasal] not at the end of a word, this occurs when followed by *ś*. (2)
That wherein duality ceases upon attainment is now explained:
from the vowels, the sibilants (*ūṣman*) and the *visarga* follow the first [consonant],
provided it is not the last letter of its class (*varga*) and stands before a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) [consonant].
The letter *ha* followed by a consonant (*sparśa*), as well as *la* and *va* followed by a consonant;

likewise, the letter *na* standing at the end of a word (*padānta*) when preceded by *ya*, *va*, or *ha*—these are the letters beginning with the sibilants (*ūṣman*) that have been described as being exempt from doubling. 4–5.
Although it has been explained in many ways by the sages who know the Vedas, that which has been adopted by all students is here declared:
[the substitution of *ya* occurs] after the letter *ṅ*, provided it is not at the end of a word, when followed by *ta* or *tha*.

It is determined that *ka* and *ga* are, respectively, the *āgama*s (augment vowels). When *m* stands before the nasals *ya*, *va*, and *la*, it acquires the homogeneous nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) when they are joined together. (7–8)

In the Taittirīyaka [Saṃhitā], when *ṣ* and *s* follow, a nasalized *ñ* replaces the *n* that precedes *ś*; provided that the preceding sound is not a sibilant (*ūṣman*) and that the following *n* is not followed by another nasal (*anuttama*). Furthermore, when a contact consonant (*sparśa*) follows a non-sibilant, the first of the following series of nasals is substituted for the last.
Those experts in the sequence of phonemes describe them in due order. Now, for the sake of accomplishing the pronunciation of the various hand-gestures (*hastavinyāsa*),
and also for the accomplishment of the unmentioned vowels such as the acute (*udātta*) and others.

A consonant is a limb (*aṅga*) of the following [vowel]; that which precedes it is considered finished. An *anusvāra*, the first part of a conjunct (*yogādi*), and a *bhakti* are likewise limbs of the following.
A vowel not homogeneous with the following is a limb of the following, as is a syllable followed by a semivowel (*antasthā*). (12)
The contact with the heat of the following consonant, as well as the determination of the position of *yama*, occurs when a vowel precedes a *repha* followed by a higher-pitched sibilant (*ūṣman*);
having understood the true nature of the vowel *ṛ*, it is indeed possible to understand this. (13)
One should know that the vowel-part (*svarabhakti*) here consists extensively of the letter *ṛ*.
Indeed, the nature of the letter *ṛ* is a fusion of four quarters; within those quarters, it should be understood that at the beginning and at the end there are the essences of vowels. 14–15.

In the middle of that which lacks the *repha*, two [parts] are to be known as consisting of consonants; for the subsequent [part] is likewise joined with the subsequent vowel-foot. These two parts, endowed with the vowel-foot, are called *svarabhakti*. 16–17.

The first part [of the vowel] occurs before the letter *ha*, and the latter part occurs before *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*. One should know that the vowel is contracted (*saṃvṛtā*) before *ha*, but otherwise it is expanded (*vivṛtā*). Furthermore, there are three modifications of the preceding vowel: shortness (*alpatva*), *i*-quality (*itva*), and *u*-quality (*utva*).

Having indeed emitted this triad, one should utter the *svarabhakti*. The *svarabhakti* following a *parāsvāra* attains the state of *pracaya*; however, when it follows a long *svāra*, it does not belong to the last [syllable], for it becomes independent as a *dhūrṣad*. 19–20.

In reality, *kāma*, *manyu*, and likewise *pāpa*—in these three preceding cases—one should understand the *svarabhakti*; the vowel *i* does not occur at all. In the case of *pu-pū-pau*, when the three preceding sounds and the following *śa-ṣa-ha* sounds are present, [the same applies].

If there is a *repha* (the letter *r*) followed by the vowel *u*, there is no *svarabhakti* [vowel-fragment]. 22. In forms such as *akāriṣam*, *caṇaḥ pūrvāḥ*, *rirīṣoḥ*, *rīriṣan*, *tāriṣaḥ*, and *tāriṣat*, if there is a *repha* followed by *u*, there is no *svarabhakti*. 23.
And the letter *la* following *haśa* shall attain the status of a *svarabhakti*.
These five— *kareṇu*, *karviṇī*, *hariṇī*, *haritā*, and *haṃsapadā*— should be known as the varieties of *svarabhakti*.
*Kareṇu* occurs when *ra* and *ha* are joined; *karviṇī* occurs when *la* and *ha* are joined;
*hariṇī* occurs when there are two *ra*s and a *sa*; and *hāritā* occurs when *la*, *sa*, and *ka* are joined.
(26) Furthermore, that which is named *haṃsapadā* consists of *repha* (*ra*) and *ṣakāra* (*ṣa*).
"In the Kāṭhaka [recension], a vowel (vāsaḥ) followed by an anusvāra is not a constituent part of the preceding [consonant];
for a contact consonant (sparśa) whose original form is a sibilant (ūṣman) cannot attain the status of being a constituent part of what precedes it.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Sarvasaṃmataśikṣāvivaraṇa* composed by Mañcanabhaṭṭa.

The section on phonemes (aṅga) is completed. Now begins the section on the arrangement of accents; here, the arrangement of the phonemes, which are the substrata of the udātta and other accents, is set forth.
The natural configuration [of the body] is described for the sake of attaining knowledge by those who lack it:
that which is this length of the body, the firmness of the limbs,
and the narrowness of the space of the throat— these are the causes for birth in a high state.
The shortness of the body, the softness of the limbs,
and the largeness of the space in the throat are the causes for birth among low-born people;
the combination of these two would be the cause for the production of the *svarita* accent.
The well-known nature of *pracaya* (the continuous rise) is that it consists solely of the audible *udātta*.
That *anudātta* which follows an *udātta* and attains the state of *svarita* is proclaimed as *tairovyañjana*, provided it is preceded by an *udātta*.
A wise person should state that even fewer [syllables] may be released from the *pāda-vṛtta*; however,
that which is proclaimed as a *pāda-vṛtta* when there is an expansion (*vivṛti*) of two feet is called *prātihata*, whereas that which is chanted in a *saṃhitā* [context] is [called] *svarya*.
In that regard, those skilled in the analysis of vowels (svaravicakṣaṇa) must exercise extreme gentleness.
In the case of a violation of metrical feet (pādavṛttahati), the *tairovyañjana* and *vādhaka* [rules] would apply;
however, when a syllable is struck by the terms *sarva* or *ava*, it does not invalidate the suffix (*pratyaya*).
The unaccented syllables following a circumflex (svarita) attain the state of *pracaya* (the monotone).
Where a circumflex and an acute (*udātta*) follow one another, if the circumflex does not occur [as a result], there the *pracaya* is also set aside.

Where the vowel *a* is elided after the letters *e* or *o*, I shall here explain in detail the rules for the preceding syllable regarding the insertion of another vowel, starting with those vowels that are inherently acute (*udātta*).
If the elided *a* is grave (*anudātta*), the preceding [acute] vowel becomes circumflex (*svarita*).
This is to be known as the *abhinihata*; the wise one should declare it to be very firm.
(12) When the vowels *i* and *u* become *ya* and *va* respectively, provided they are acute (*udātta*), that which follows them is indeed the circumflex (*svarita*) when it is grave (*nīca*). (13)

By name, however, this would indeed be *kṣaipra*; one should state it more firmly when the vowel *u* is high-pitched (*udātta*) and the following vowel *u* is low-pitched (*anudātta*). In this case, the *ū* being produced through their combination becomes a *svarita* sandhi.
Even when joined together, a wise person should speak very softly when this [vowel] is taught.

Where a vowel situated at the end of a word is pronounced with a *yama* sound, preceded by a low tone (*nīca*) or otherwise unprecedented (*apūrva*), it is constant; there the wise person should speak more firmly.
Even when preceded by a high syllable at the end of another foot, it is always [a *pādavṛtta*] and not otherwise.
(17) If that which is devoid of the aforementioned characteristics is accented (*svarita*) anywhere, even if it possesses little *vāyu*, it is declared to be a *pādavṛtta*. (18)

When a vowel preceding *nāda* or *anusvāra* is situated as *svarita*, there is no suppression (*ākṣepa*) of that vowel; in the case of *nāda*, it is indeed *anusvāra*. However, for the fifth [class of consonants] at the pause (*virāma*), the designation *nāda* is proclaimed.
Where there is one middle *madhya* and a low (*nīca*) *vikrama*, that is declared [to be] *svarita*.

A wise person should pronounce the *vikrama* very firmly; and when a *svarita* follows, the latter half of that *svarita* [is also firm]. 20. When a *svarita* occurs as the subsequent element, [the first half of] the *svarita* [is low].
One should make it low and trembling, and one should utter it long;
in the middle, however, one should cause a tremor, and one should pronounce both sides equally.
Of these two, there should be one here, and therein also the vowel is said [to be applied].

If one of those two is unaccented (anudātta) and the other is indeed high-pitched (udātta), then in their conjunction there shall indeed be a circumflex (svarita) accent. A word containing a single udātta is to be known as having one udātta; a word containing a pair of udāttas is to be known as having two udāttas.

One should know that a word may have three udātta accents, or another may be always svarita; or else, among words, a word may sometimes be entirely anudātta. A compound word would be tri-udātta [if it contains] one udātta and two udāttas.

Whatever else is beneficial among these is indeed low; such is the established position of the word-form as declared by the learned. However, regarding the Vedic [form], this occurs later at the time of the word, precisely upon the prior utterance. 27–28.

A prefix (*upasarga*) standing at the end of a word, as well as a low-pitched vowel (*nīca*) preceding two [consonants], and likewise a vowel situated in the middle of three [consonants], as well as *avāna* and *avagraha*, [are not subject to doubling]. Furthermore, [the following prefixes are treated similarly]:
*prā*, *āpā*, *anvā*, *abhi*, *pari*, *ut*, *su*, *vi*, *ati*, *ni*, *adhi*, *api*, *upa*, and *prati*. 29.
In this [section], seven upasargas are traditionally recorded as twelve.

"Māstām" [is the first] with the word "mahitvanā"; "priya-dhā" [is the second]; "viśat" [is the third]; "puṇaḥ moṣūṇaḥ" [is the fourth]; "ca" [is the fifth]; "aryamā yāti" [is the sixth]; and "pūṣā adhatta api adhatta yat" [is the seventh]. 30–31.
Having become "the sacrificial fee turns back" (*dakṣiṇā vartate*) and so forth, and having become the *ṛc* verses such as "place it" (*āsādayati*), she enters into each and every person;
having performed these three steps, she is said to take away, bestow, and obtain. 32.
There are twenty [cases] such as "dadhnā tanakti" and "codgātā rohati.
One should recognize that as a *trikrama* where an *āṅ* ending in long *ā* and having an acute accent (*udātta*) is seen followed by another vowel, as in "mūṣūṇa" and "ūṣuṇaḥ. (33–34)
In the sequence of the *saṃhitā*, one should pronounce the preceding and following [words] as if they were independent words;
that which is elided in the *krama* and is subject to *pragṛhya* rules should be pronounced twice in the middle.
Furthermore, whatever is marked with a nod (*iṅgya*) and elided in the *krama*, and that which constitutes a pause (*avasāna*), should both be pronounced twice. (35)
The semi-vowels (*antasthā*) and the labial class (*pavarga*) are situated before the vowels;
*triṣṭubh* and *anuṣṭubh* meters are likewise mentioned, and these two [syllables] are declared to end in the letter *ka*.
However, elsewhere it is certain that these two end in the letter *pa*.
However, the established rule is that in that case there is a reversal of the preceding injunction (37).
Whether there is a pause between two consonants or between two vowels, or between labial sounds,
the wise man should utter the subsequent sound with the articulatory effort (*prayatna*) of the preceding sound (38).

When the vowel *au* follows, as well as when *va* follows, one should know that the *ha* of the chest [belongs to the preceding vowel]; likewise, when the semivowels (*antasthā*) follow, and when the subsequent [vowels] follow, there is this additional nasalization (*nāsikyattva*) here. 39.
One should not emit the breath excessively through the nostrils during the conjunction with the syllable *ha*;
nor should one speak excessively with the chest during the conjunction with the semi-vowels (*antasthā*). A protracted vowel situated at the end of a word is nasalized and is designated as *raṅga*.
In the *Kāṭhaka*, they know four long vowels as being colored; in the *Āraṇyaka*, there are five colors. In the *Taittirīyaka*, there are four long vowels that are protracted (*pluta*):
in the verses, the auspicious ones, and those containing the syllable *yat*, the *upahūta* [formula], and *mama*. These are the protracted vowels. 41–42.
The *nāsikya*, the final *anusvāra*, the semivowels (*antasthā*), the letter *ha*, and the vowels are always nasalized (*nāsikya*) by virtue of their cause.
The effort (*prayatna*) for the vowels and the sibilants (*ūṣman*) is traditionally held to be wide-open (*vivṛta*).
This specific quality of being "closed" (saṃvṛta) is prescribed for the letter *a*.

One should know that the contact (spṛṣṭatā) of the stops (sparśas) is [complete]; in the semivowels (antasthās), it is slightly uttered; and in the fourth class [the sibilants], the wise should understand the contact to be like the rim of a wheel.

Where there is a conjunction of consonants (*sparśa*) in the recitation, if it occurs thus, then there is no audible sound for the initial [consonant] of those two, nor for a consonant at the pause (*virāma*). Furthermore, at the end of a word (*padānta*), when followed by a consonant of the *ekavarga* group at the beginning of the next word, [the same applies] at the pause. (46)
A wise person should not pronounce the subsequent sound with the same articulatory effort as the preceding one.
(47) When there is a conjunction with the *pra* of *pravarga*, a separate effort is not required;
in that case, the pause (*virāma*) has the duration of one *mātrā*, whereas elsewhere it has the duration of two *mātrās*. (48)

In the *saṃhitā*, wherever there is a phonetic combination (*sāṃhita*) that functions like a word (*padavat*), that should be understood as the *prakṛti* (base form); through knowledge alone one obtains the fruit.
[This applies] when the first letter is the fourth, the seventh, or likewise the tenth.
Among these twelve vowels, the duration of one *mātrā* is proclaimed [for the first four].
The second, the fifth, the eighth, the eleventh, and the four beginning with the thirteenth are proclaimed to have a duration of two *mātrās*. 50–51.
The sixth [syllable] of the third [pāda] of the ninth [chapter] shall be protracted (pluta).

The letter *la* shall consist of three quarters; however, for the fifth [syllables], the duration is proclaimed to be one mora (mātrika) from both short and long vowels, as well as from the protracted.
The duration of the five [consonants] standing upon a short vowel is two mātrās;
in the hiatus (vivṛtti) between words, it is proclaimed to be one mātrā. It is certain that in the hiatus within a word, it shall be half a mātrā. 54.
The [syllable] beginning with a short vowel is like a calf following its mother; it is called *vatsānusāriṇī*.
(55) The doubling (*vivṛttatva*) occurs within a word, and its duration is determined by the capacity [of the preceding sound], being half a *mātrā* in the case of *pragrahas*. (56)
Because they are applied with the effort of grasping [the meaning], it is clear that there is oneness of the *pāda*; thus everyone performs their recitation by adopting the oneness of the *pada*.
Otherwise, like a *ṛc* verse, it would be something exceeding the mere number, and like a *pada*, it would be [merely a sequence of syllables].
It is certain that at the end [of a word], syllables possess a duration of two mātrās (58).
When an anusvāra is followed by a conjunct consonant, its duration is one mātrā; otherwise, it is proclaimed as having two mātrās by all students (59).

An *anusvāra* has a duration of two morae (*dvimātra*) when followed by a *repha* (the sound *r*) or a sibilant (*ūṣman*). However, when followed by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), it should have one mora (*mātrika*), provided it possesses a double form.
If the initial member of a conjunct consonant stands between two labial vowels, [it is treated as having a single mora].
After a *visarga* followed by a *kṣa* or *ra*, [the pause] in both cases consists of half a *mātrā*.
However, in the middle of a word (*ilamadhye*), the duration of time is proclaimed to be half a *mātrā*.
At the end of a word (*bhakti*), it would be half a *mātrā*; at the end of a sentence (*vākyānte*), it is one and a half *mātrās*.
At the end of an *avagraha*, however, the duration is proclaimed to be one *mātrā*;
at the end of a half-verse of a *ṛc*, it is declared to be three *mātrās*.
A nasalized sound (*nāsikya*) situated between two manifest consonants shall have a duration of one and a quarter *mātrās*.

At the conclusion of an *anuvāka*, five *mātrās* are prescribed; at the conclusion of an *aṣṭaka* and a *daśaka*, it should be understood as eight and ten respectively, according to the sequence in the *praśna* and *kāṇḍa*;
however, at the conclusion of the *tantras*, a period of three days is required.
A learned man, remaining vigilant at both the beginning and the conclusion of the Veda,
should clearly utter the *praṇava* for the protection of the sacred hymns; for if it is not uttered at the outset, the Veda flows away, and if not at the end, it falls apart.
In the Yajurveda, the *praṇava* (Oṃ) should be pronounced loudly (*uccaiḥ*). The *svāra* accents occur at the beginning of those [sections] where Oṃ is placed.

(67) The introductory [syllable] within the Veda should consist of four *mātrās*. That which follows it consists of half that [two *mātrās*]. At the end of a chapter (*adhyāya*), the end of an *anuvāka*, and at the beginning of a ritual action (*karman*), it consists of three *mātrās*. (68)
The primordial sound (nāda), beginning from its inception, proceeds through stages consisting of measures (mātrā) and atoms (aṇu);
it exists within the Veda in the syllable *praṇava*, where there is a state of two measures in the letter *ma*.
A consonant, being eternally without vowel-sound, is employed as having the measure of an atom.
And because of their frequent association with those who have increased their [vocal] measures, it has been proclaimed thus:
"The blue jay cries with one measure, the crow with two measures, and the peacock cries with three measures; such is the definition of the measures and so forth. (70–71)
Slow, fast, and medium—these are indeed the three modes of speech.
When there is a difference in the mode, a clear difference in duration occurs with respect to the action.
That effort which has been described as being equal for someone in all cases remains so for them.

Indeed, that equality of effort is called equality of tempo (vṛttisāmya). By whatever tempo one begins the recitation, one should continue in that very same manner until the pause; this is what is called equality of tempo.

Relying upon the middle mode of pronunciation (*madhyamā vṛtti*), the determination of the [temporal] durations has been established in the Prātiśākhya and other treatises; for that very mode is what is adopted there.
Furthermore, *vikrama* is prescribed for the middle of a word (*padamadhye*) and for the middle of a nasalized vowel (*iṅgyamadhye*).
The *vikrama* (the pause) is prescribed at the end of a sentence and at the end of a word.
A wise person should always place the prefix (*pra*) in connection with the following word,
and likewise, he should always place the prefix (*pari*) in connection with the preceding word.

One who sings, one who reads too fast, one who shakes the head, one who reads exactly as written, one who understands the meaning incorrectly, and one with a weak voice— these six are the lowest of reciters.
(78) That which has clearly articulated syllables, that which possesses sweetness, and that which is well-composed...
Clear articulation of word-divisions, that which is endowed with steadfastness,
proficiency in tempo (laya), and purity of tone— these six qualities indeed have been prescribed for the reciter. 79–80.

The acute (udātta) belongs to the Brāhmaṇa caste; the grave (nīca) is said to belong to the Kṣatriya; the circumflex (svarita) belongs to the Vaiśya caste, and the protracted (pracaya) is declared to be the Śūdra.
(81) The first letters of the consonant classes and the vowels are of the Brāhmaṇa caste.
The second, third, and fourth classes of the *kṣatra* caste, as well as the semivowels (*antastha*) and the sibilants (*uttama*), are indeed declared to be the *vaiśya* castes;
while the *anusvāra*, the *visarga*, and the aspirates (*ūṣman*) are the *śūdra* castes. (82–83)
Indeed, with the right hand shaped like a cow’s ear, one should indicate the vowel while fixing the gaze on the tip of the hand, contemplating the meaning of the scripture;
however, one should not do so with all the fingers, but rather with the thumb alone. 84.
Abandoning the shaking of the head, the placement of the musical notes (svaranyāsa) is prescribed as follows:
one should indicate the low notes (mandra-svara), starting from the little finger, by placing the middle joints of the ring finger, the middle finger, and the index finger respectively. 85–86.
When *na* is at the end of a word and *ya*, *va*, or *ha* follow, and when those two—
namely *na* and *ya*— are joined together, their conjunction is not perceived during the pronunciations of the phonemes; such is the extent of what has been declared regarding the *sāman*.
One should utter [the mantra] with devotion to Brahman, neither deficient nor excessive.
Just as a tigress carries her cub with her fangs without causing it pain—fearing both its falling and its being crushed—one should likewise employ the phonemes. 88–89.
One should direct the phonemes in such a way that they are neither too distinct nor too indistinct,
like a vessel full of milk, with a steady gaze and according to one's ability;
one should utter them at all times with supreme devotion and without sloth.
Since any lapse in their birth [of the mantras] is equivalent to the killing of that very birth; 91.
One who has fallen away from the hand, fallen from the accent, likewise from the phoneme, from the time, from the meaning, and from the ritual application, does not enjoy the fruit of the Veda. 92.
But he who studies [the Veda] devoid of its hands— that is, bereft of proper accent, phoneme, and meaning— is consumed by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman verses and enters a low womb.
A mantra deficient in accent or phoneme, when incorrectly employed, does not convey its intended meaning.
That thunderbolt of speech destroys the sacrificer, just as Indra’s enemy [did] due to a lapse in the accent (94).
It has been declared in various places that he who utters [the mantra] correctly, clearly perceiving the accents and phonemes, attains the most excellent fruit (95).
He who studies the Veda with his hand [in the prescribed manner], endowed with correct accents, phonemes, and meanings,
is purified by the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman verses and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
(96) One who knows the specific distinctions of the *pada-pāṭha* and *krama-pāṭha*, and is skilled in the sequence of phonemes—
One who knows the divisions of vowels, measures, and so forth, should go to the assembly of teachers.
This universally accepted *Lakṣaṇa* was composed by the high-souled Keśavārya, the son of Budhendranandana, for the sake of Sūryadeva. 97–98.
Thus ends the training approved by all.
